library(ggplot2)

# From Perfect Mirror to Average Mirror

In the idealized world the matrix \( M \) satisfied \( M = M^\top \) exactly.  
In the real world edges are added and removed, directions flip, measurements are noisy. The instantaneous adjacency matrix is almost never symmetric.

Yet if we look at a long-run average — the density of visits, the time-averaged connection strength, the histogram of a chaotic orbit — a clear mirror symmetry can reappear. That is **symmetry on average**.

This is the idea from a classic paper *Symmetric Chaos*, by Frame and Golubitsky:

{{< pdf https://www.asc.ohio-state.edu/golubitsky.4/reprintweb-0.5/output/papers/symmetric_chaos.pdf >}}

## Noisy adjacency that still averages to a mirror

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-cap: "Instantaneous noisy matrix versus its long-run average"

# ideal mirror
ideal <- matrix(0, 6, 6)
ideal[1, 2] <- ideal[2, 1] <- 1
ideal[2, 3] <- ideal[3, 2] <- 1
ideal[3, 4] <- ideal[4, 3] <- 1
ideal[4, 5] <- ideal[5, 4] <- 1
ideal[5, 6] <- ideal[6, 5] <- 1
ideal[6, 1] <- ideal[1, 6] <- 1

# many noisy realizations
n_real <- 200
avg <- matrix(0, 6, 6)
for (k in 1:n_real) {
  noise <- matrix(rbinom(36, 1, 0.08), 6, 6)
  noisy <- pmax(0, pmin(1, ideal + noise - matrix(rbinom(36, 1, 0.08), 6, 6)))
  avg <- avg + noisy
}
avg <- avg / n_real

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
image(t(ideal[6:1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = c("white", "steelblue"),
      main = "Ideal mirror")
image(t(noisy[6:1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = c("white", "firebrick"),
      main = "One noisy snapshot")
image(t(avg[6:1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(20, "Blues"),
      main = "Average over 200 snapshots")
```

## Field and Golubitsky’s Design Method

Field and Golubitsky generate symmetric images by iterating a map that is *equivariant* under a chosen symmetry group (usually a cyclic or dihedral group of order \( m \)).  

The basic family of maps (in the complex plane) takes the form

\[
z \mapsto \bigl(\lambda + \alpha |z|^2 + \beta \operatorname{Re}(z^m) + i\omega\bigr) z + \gamma \overline{z}^{m-1}.
\]

- The polynomial is constructed so that it *commutes* with rotation by \( 2\pi/m \) (and, when \( \omega = 0 \), with reflections). That is the mathematical embodiment of the symmetry: if \( z \) is on the attractor then so is every rotated (and reflected) copy.
- Iteration of the map is chaotic for many parameter values: a single trajectory wanders aperiodically and never settles into a periodic orbit that itself possesses the symmetry.
- The *density* of a long trajectory (how often the orbit visits each pixel) nevertheless inherits the full symmetry of the map. Colouring by visit count therefore produces a picture whose symmetry is visible only “on average.”

This is precisely the passage from an idealized mirror constraint to symmetry-on-average in the presence of chaotic “noise.”

### Emperor’s Cloak (pentagonal, \( m = 5 \))

A classic example uses the reduced form in which \( \alpha = -\lambda \) (the complex logistic map plus a symmetry-breaking term):

\[
z \mapsto (\lambda - \lambda |z|^2) z + \gamma \overline{z}^{4}.
\]

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-cap: "Emperor’s Cloak — density of a 5-fold equivariant map"
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
#| 

emperors_cloak <- function(z, lambda = -1.81, gamma = 1) {
  r2 <- Mod(z)^2
  (lambda - lambda * r2) * z + gamma * Conj(z)^4
}

n <- 150000
z <- 0.1 + 0.2i
pts <- complex(n)
for (i in 1:n) {
  z <- emperors_cloak(z)
  pts[i] <- z
}
pts <- pts[-(1:2000)]
pts <- pts[abs(pts) < 1.5]

df <- data.frame(x = Re(pts), y = Im(pts))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  stat_bin2d(bins = 80) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", trans = "log10", na.value = "black") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA))
```



```{r}
#| label: fig-emperors-cloak
#| fig-cap: "The Emperor's Cloak symmetric icon (Field & Golubitsky)."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: true
#| message: false

library(grid)

# --- Parameters: Emperor's Cloak ---------------------------------------
n      <- 5
lambda <- -1.806
alpha  <-  1.806
beta   <-  0
omega  <-  0
gamma  <-  1

cloak_step <- function(z) {
  (lambda + alpha * (Re(z)^2 + Im(z)^2) + beta * Re(z^n) + 1i * omega) * z +
    gamma * Conj(z)^(n - 1)
}

# --- Many orbits in parallel -------------------------------------------
set.seed(1)
n_orbits <- 20000
z <- complex(real = rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1),
             imaginary = rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1))
for (i in 1:500) z <- cloak_step(z)           # burn-in

# --- Pass 1: bounds -----------------------------------------------------
L  <- 0
zz <- z
for (i in 1:300) {
  zz <- cloak_step(zz)
  L  <- max(L, abs(Re(zz)), abs(Im(zz)))
}
L <- L * 1.05

# --- Pass 2: 2D histogram ----------------------------------------------
N      <- 800
counts <- numeric(N * N)
for (i in 1:1000) {
  z  <- cloak_step(z)
  ix <- floor((Re(z) + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L
  iy <- floor((Im(z) + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L
  ok <- is.finite(ix) & is.finite(iy) & ix >= 1L & ix <= N & iy >= 1L & iy <= N
  counts <- counts + tabulate((iy[ok] - 1L) * N + ix[ok], nbins = N * N)
}

# --- Density -> colour --------------------------------------------------
d     <- log1p(counts) / log1p(quantile(counts[counts > 0], 0.999))
d     <- pmin(d, 1)
stops <- c(0, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50, 0.72, 1)
pal   <- col2rgb(c("black", "#FFE9FF", "yellow", "red", "#00D600", "white"))
ch    <- lapply(1:3, function(k) approx(stops, pal[k, ], xout = d)$y)
cols  <- rgb(ch[[1]], ch[[2]], ch[[3]], maxColorValue = 255)

img <- t(matrix(cols, N, N))[N:1, ]           # rows = y (top first), cols = x

# --- Draw on the active device (Quarto captures this) ------------------
grid.newpage()
grid.raster(img, interpolate = FALSE)

```
```{r}
#| label: fig-emperors-cloak-symengine
#| fig-cap: "The Emperor's Cloak, built with symengine and drawn with ggplot2."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
#| 

library(symengine)
library(ggplot2)

# --- Parameters: Emperor's Cloak ---------------------------------------
n <- 5; lambda <- -1.806; alpha <- 1.806; beta <- 0; omega <- 0; gamma <- 1

# --- Symbolic map, using real/imaginary pairs --------------------------
x <- S("x"); y <- S("y")
cmul <- function(a, b) list(re = a$re * b$re - a$im * b$im,
                            im = a$re * b$im + a$im * b$re)
cpow <- function(a, k) {
  r <- list(re = S("1"), im = S("0"))
  for (i in seq_len(k)) r <- cmul(r, a)
  r
}

zn  <- cpow(list(re = x, im =  y), n)        # z^n
zc1 <- cpow(list(re = x, im = -y), n - 1)    # conj(z)^(n-1)

p  <- lambda + alpha * (x^2 + y^2) + beta * zn$re
fx <- expand(p * x - omega * y + gamma * zc1$re)
fy <- expand(p * y + omega * x + gamma * zc1$im)

fx; fy   # inspect the expanded polynomials (optional)

# --- Turn the symbolic polynomials into plain R functions ---------------
to_r_fun <- function(expr) {
  e <- parse(text = as.character(expr))[[1]]    # "**" parses as "^" in R
  function(x, y) eval(e, list(x = x, y = y))
}
f_x <- to_r_fun(fx)
f_y <- to_r_fun(fy)

# Quick check against a direct complex-number calculation (optional)
z0 <- complex(real = 0.3, imaginary = -0.2)
z1 <- (lambda + alpha * Mod(z0)^2 + beta * Re(z0^n) + 1i * omega) * z0 +
  gamma * Conj(z0)^(n - 1)
all.equal(c(f_x(0.3, -0.2), f_y(0.3, -0.2)), c(Re(z1), Im(z1)))

# --- Many orbits in parallel -------------------------------------------
set.seed(1)
n_orbits <- 20000
px <- rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1)
py <- rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1)

iterate <- function() {
  nx <- f_x(x = px, y = py)
  ny <- f_y(x = px, y = py)
  px <<- nx; py <<- ny
}
for (i in 1:500) iterate()                    # burn-in

# Pass 1: bounds
L <- 0
sx <- px; sy <- py
for (i in 1:300) {
  nx <- f_x(x = sx, y = sy); ny <- f_y(x = sx, y = sy)
  sx <- nx; sy <- ny
  L <- max(L, abs(sx), abs(sy))
}
L <- L * 1.05

# Pass 2: 2D histogram
N <- 800
counts <- numeric(N * N)
for (i in 1:1000) {
  iterate()
  ix <- floor((px + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L
  iy <- floor((py + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L
  ok <- is.finite(ix) & is.finite(iy) & ix >= 1L & ix <= N & iy >= 1L & iy <= N
  counts <- counts + tabulate((iy[ok] - 1L) * N + ix[ok], nbins = N * N)
}

# --- ggplot2 -------------------------------------------------------------
centres <- seq(-L, L, length.out = N + 1)[-1] - L / N
cloak <- data.frame(
  x = rep(centres, times = N),     # ix varies fastest, matching the count index
  y = rep(centres, each  = N),
  d = pmin(1, log1p(counts) / log1p(quantile(counts[counts > 0], 0.999)))
)

ggplot(cloak, aes(x, y, fill = d)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("black", "#FFE9FF", "yellow", "red", "#00D600", "white"),
    values  = c(0, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50, 0.72, 1),
    limits  = c(0, 1), guide = "none"
  ) +
  coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", colour = NA))
```



### p5.js: live Emperor’s Cloak

```{=html}
<div id="emperors-cloak"></div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/p5@1.9.0/lib/p5.min.js"></script>
<script>
new p5((p) => {
  let z, density;
  const m = 5, lambda = -1.81, gamma = 1;
  p.setup = () => {
    p.createCanvas(420, 420);
    density = p.createGraphics(420, 420);
    density.background(0);
    density.colorMode(p.HSB, 255);
    z = p.createVector(0.1, 0.2);
  };
  p.draw = () => {
    for (let i = 0; i < 250; i++) {
      let x = z.x, y = z.y;
      let r2 = x*x + y*y;
      // (λ - λ r²) z
      let nx = (lambda - lambda * r2) * x;
      let ny = (lambda - lambda * r2) * y;
      // + γ conj(z)^{m-1}
      let ang = p.atan2(y, x);
      let mag = p.sqrt(r2);
      let ang2 = -ang * (m - 1);
      let mag2 = p.pow(mag, m - 1);
      nx += gamma * mag2 * p.cos(ang2);
      ny += gamma * mag2 * p.sin(ang2);
      z.set(nx, ny);
      let px = p.map(z.x, -1.4, 1.4, 10, 410);
      let py = p.map(z.y, -1.4, 1.4, 10, 410);
      density.stroke((p.frameCount * 0.4) % 255, 200, 255, 30);
      density.point(px, py);
    }
    p.image(density, 0, 0);
  };
}, document.getElementById("emperors-cloak"));
</script>
<p><em>Emperor’s Cloak accumulating in real time. The five-fold symmetry appears only in the density.</em></p>
```

### A second design (triangular symmetry)

The same construction with \( m = 3 \) and different coefficients yields a triangular icon.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Triangular symmetric icon (m = 3)"

icon3 <- function(z, lambda = 1.5, alpha = -1.0, gamma = -0.8) {
  r2 <- Mod(z)^2
  (lambda + alpha * r2) * z + gamma * Conj(z)^2
}

n <- 100000
z <- 0.2 + 0.1i
pts <- complex(n)
for (i in 1:n) {
  z <- icon3(z)
  pts[i] <- z
}
pts <- pts[-(1:1000)]
pts <- pts[abs(pts) < 1.6]

df <- data.frame(x = Re(pts), y = Im(pts))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  stat_bin2d(bins = 70) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "log10", na.value = "black") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA))
```

The choice of the equivariant polynomial fixes the mathematical symmetry; the chaotic iteration supplies the randomness; the coloured density reveals the symmetry on average. That is the entire Field–Golubitsky design pipeline.

# The Three-World Summary

| World              | Matrix relation       | Visual character                  |
|--------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Graphs & adjacency | \( A \) arbitrary     | Directed, possibly one-way        |
| Idealized mirror   | \( M = M^\top \) exactly | Perfect bilateral / dihedral     |
| Real world         | \( \mathbb{E}[A] \approx M \) | Symmetry visible only on average |

The artistic and design lesson is unchanged from the Field–Golubitsky pictures:  
you may design with an equivariant rule (a “mirror” constraint) even when the underlying process is noisy or chaotic. The long-term image, the density, the average, will still carry the symmetry you imposed.  

That is the practical bridge between the clean adjacency algebra and the hurly-burly of generative art.
